questions.text: Architect C's building design was widely photographed and published on architecture websites without authorization. The unauthorized use occurred for 5 years before the architect became aware. What remedy is most appropriate under RA 8293?

options.text: The architect must accept the unauthorized use because publication occurred more than 3 years prior, and the statute of limitations may apply
The architect can pursue injunctive relief to stop ongoing infringement and recover damages for past unauthorized use under RA 8293
The architect can only demand removal of the photographs; monetary damages are not available for web publication, as digital use is often considered fair use
The statute of limitations has expired, preventing any legal action after 5 years of use, unless continuous infringement can be proven

rationale.a: Falsely imposes a statute of limitations based on duration of use; no time bar eliminates rights to stop ongoing infringement.
rationale.c: Incorrectly limits remedies to removal; copyright infringement includes the right to recover monetary damages for lost fees and profits.
rationale.d: Misapplies statute of limitations; the architecture infringement can be remedied even after years of unauthorized use, and ongoing use remains actionable.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 protects reproduction and public display rights, which extend to photographs and website publication of architectural works without authorization. The architect may pursue injunctive relief to halt ongoing infringement and recover damages for past unauthorized use. The length of prior unauthorized use does not eliminate the architect's remedies. Philippine intellectual property law provides generous damages provisions in infringement cases.
rationale.takeaway: An architect can pursue injunctions and damages for unauthorized publication of architectural works regardless of how long the infringement continued.

questions.text: Architect A created a distinctive hotel design with a unique curved facade and innovative interior spatial flow. Architect B, without authorization, created a new building with an identical curved facade and nearly identical interior spatial arrangement. Can Architect A pursue infringement remedies under RA 8293?

options.text: No, because buildings are functional structures that cannot be protected by copyright, unless they contain significant artistic elements
Yes, if Architect A can prove Architect B copied the specific creative expression, not merely the functional concept
Only if Architect A had registered the design with IPOPHL before Architect B's work began, ensuring legal protection under intellectual property laws
No, because the functional building code requirements make the design inherently non-protected, unless it can be shown to have artistic merit

rationale.a: Falsely assumes all buildings are unprotectable; copyright protects the creative expression embodied in the building, even though buildings are functional.
rationale.c: Confuses evidentiary advantage with a requirement for infringement; copyright exists and infringement can be proven without registration.
rationale.d: Overgeneralizes copyright limitations; code-mandated functional elements are unprotected, but distinctive creative choices are protected.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 protects original creative expression in architectural works. The distinctive curved facade and innovative spatial arrangement are protectable creative elements. If the evidence shows copying of these specific creative features rather than independent design based on similar functional requirements, infringement remedies are available. Registration provides evidentiary advantage but is not required for infringement to exist.
rationale.takeaway: Identical copying of distinctive creative design features (facade, spatial flow) constitutes infringement; functional similarity alone does not.

questions.text: What does RA 8293 protect in an architectural design?

options.text: Only the functional arrangement of rooms required by building codes, without regard to aesthetic elements
Only the construction method and structural system used, excluding any creative or artistic aspects
The architect's original creative expression in spatial design, aesthetic treatment, and distinctive conceptualization
The cost estimate and project schedule developed by the architect, including all financial projections

rationale.a: Confuses copyright scope with building code compliance; functional requirements are not protected because they are dictated by code, not creative choice.
rationale.b: Misunderstands copyrightability; standard construction methods are not protected because they are functional and not creative expression.
rationale.d: Extends protection beyond copyright scope; costs and schedules are project management documents, not creative design subject to copyright.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 copyright protects the original creative expression in architectural designs, including distinctive spatial arrangements, aesthetic treatments, facade proportions, and unique structural conceptualizations. It does not protect functional elements mandated by building codes or common construction methods used by many architects.
rationale.takeaway: Copyright protects the architect's creative design choices and aesthetic expression, not purely functional or code-mandated elements.

questions.text: How long does copyright protection for architectural works extend under RA 8293?

options.text: For 20 years from the date the design is first created and registered with the Intellectual Property Office
For the lifetime of the architect plus 50 years after the architect's death
For 50 years from the date the building is completed and granted a certificate of occupancy
Only for 10 years unless the building remains in continuous use and the architect renews registration

rationale.a: Drastically shortens the protection period and misdates the measurement from creation instead of death; RA 8293 provides much longer protection.
rationale.c: Measures from building completion instead of the architect's death and provides only 50 years instead of life plus 50 years.
rationale.d: Imposes an arbitrary short term and a false dependency on continuous building use; copyright term does not depend on building occupation.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 provides copyright protection for architectural works for the life of the architect plus 70 years (RA 8293 Sec 213 as amended by RA 10372) following the architect's death. This extended protection period reflects the long-term value of architectural intellectual property. For corporate authors, protection runs for 50 years from first publication. The term does not depend on building completion or continuous use.
rationale.takeaway: Copyright in architectural works extends for the architect's lifetime plus 50 years post-mortem, not limited by creation or completion dates.

questions.text: Under RA 8293, when does copyright protection attach to an architectural design or building?

options.text: Only after the architect registers the copyright with IPOPHL, ensuring that all legal documentation is properly filed and acknowledged
Only after the building is completed and occupied, which signifies the practical realization of the design in a tangible form
Automatically when the work is fixed in a tangible medium, without need for registration or notice
Only if the architect publishes the design in a professional journal, thereby making it publicly accessible and recognized within the professional community

rationale.a: Confuses registration as an evidentiary aid with a requirement for copyright to exist; copyright arises by operation of law upon creation.
rationale.b: Incorrectly requires building completion; copyright attaches to the design when fixed in drawings, regardless of whether construction ever occurs.
rationale.d: Falsely requires publication; copyright exists automatically without any form of publication or notice.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 provides automatic copyright protection upon fixation of the work in a tangible medium (drawings, specifications, constructed building). Registration with IPOPHL is not required for copyright to exist; however, registration provides evidentiary advantages in enforcing the copyright. No copyright notice is legally required.
rationale.takeaway: Copyright in architectural works exists automatically upon creation and fixation in tangible form; registration is optional but provides evidentiary benefits.

questions.text: An architect created distinctive building designs in 1990. The architect died in 2015. Under RA 8293, when does copyright in these works expire?

options.text: In 2040 (25 years after creation), which is a common misconception about copyright duration
In 2035 (20 years after creation), often confused with patent durations
In 2085 (70 years after the architect's death per RA 8293 as amended by RA 10372 Sec 213.1)
Copyright in architectural works never expires under Philippine law, a misunderstanding of copyright principles

rationale.a: Incorrectly measures from creation date instead of death and provides only 25 years instead of life plus 50 years post-mortem.
rationale.b: Measures from creation instead of death and provides only 20 years total; RA 8293 provides much longer protection.
rationale.d: Falsely claims perpetual copyright; while protection is long (lifetime plus 50 years), it eventually expires.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 provides that copyright extends for the life of the author plus 50 years after death. The architect created works in 1990 and died in 2015. Copyright protection continues for 50 years after 2015, expiring in 2065. The date of creation is relevant only for works by corporate authors; for individual authors, the death date determines the post-mortem protection period.
rationale.takeaway: For individual architects, copyright expires 50 years after the architect's death, not based on creation or building completion dates.

questions.text: An architect's work is automatically protected by copyright under RA 8293, yet the architect chooses to register the work with IPOPHL. What is the primary advantage of registration?

options.text: Registration extends the copyright protection period beyond 50 years post-mortem, allowing heirs to benefit from royalties indefinitely
Registration creates a public record and provides prima facie evidence of authorship and ownership, strengthening enforcement in infringement disputes
Registration allows the architect to sue for infringement; without registration, the architect cannot file suit, even if the work is widely copied
Registration gives the architect exclusive rights to build projects based on the design, preventing others from using similar concepts

rationale.a: Falsely claims registration extends the protection term; the statutory term is the same whether registered or not.
rationale.c: Incorrectly requires registration to sue; unregistered copyrights are still enforceable, though with heavier evidentiary burden.
rationale.d: Confuses copyright protection with exclusive building rights; copyright gives reproduction rights, not exclusive construction authority.
rationale.correct: Although copyright exists automatically, IPOPHL registration creates a public record of ownership and date of creation. The registered certificate constitutes prima facie evidence of the architect's authorship and copyright validity in Philippine courts, significantly strengthening the architect's position in enforcing copyright against infringers. Unregistered copyrights are still enforceable, but the burden of proof is heavier.
rationale.takeaway: IPOPHL registration provides evidentiary advantages in court but is not required for copyright to exist or be enforceable.

questions.text: An architect's moral rights under RA 8293 include the right to be credited as the author and the right to object to distortions of the work. Which scenario constitutes a violation of moral rights?

options.text: building owner performs routine maintenance that requires replacement of worn exterior wall finishes, which is generally considered acceptable under standard maintenance practices
building owner adds air conditioning systems to interior spaces by running conduits along original walls, potentially altering the aesthetic intent of the architect's design
building owner removes the architect's name plaque from the entrance and sells the building without disclosing the original architect
building owner installs new windows to improve energy efficiency while maintaining the original mullion pattern, which is typically seen as an enhancement rather than a distortion

rationale.a: Represents routine maintenance necessary for building preservation; replacing worn finishes to the same specifications does not distort the design.
rationale.b: Reflects necessary functional additions to accommodate modern systems; adding building systems without altering design character does not violate integrity rights.
rationale.d: Demonstrates responsible maintenance for efficiency; upgrading windows while preserving the architectural mullion pattern maintains design integrity.
rationale.correct: Removing attribution credit violates the architect's right of attribution. Routine maintenance, functional modifications to accommodate building systems, and energy efficiency upgrades that preserve design integrity do not violate moral rights. However, removing the architect's name without consent violates the right to be recognized as the author of the work.
rationale.takeaway: The architect's right of attribution is violated when credit is removed or not given; routine maintenance and functional upgrades preserving design integrity do not infringe moral rights.

questions.text: How do RA 9266 Section 33 and RA 8293 work together in protecting architectural intellectual property?

options.text: They are mutually exclusive; an architect must choose which statute to rely on in each case
RA 9266 is the exclusive legal basis for protecting architectural copyright in the Philippines
RA 9266 establishes that architects own copyright in their professional work; RA 8293 provides the substantive copyright framework, term of protection, moral rights, and enforcement remedies
RA 8293 applies only to copyrighted literary works, not architectural designs

rationale.a: Misunderstands the complementary relationship; the statutes work together, not exclusively.
rationale.b: Overstates RA 9266's scope; it is profession-specific, while RA 8293 is the comprehensive IP law providing remedies and procedures.
rationale.d: Incorrectly restricts RA 8293 to literary works; it explicitly protects architectural works and other creative expressions.
rationale.correct: Both statutes protect architectural intellectual property but serve complementary functions. RA 9266 Section 33(1) requires architects to include copyright ownership notice in service agreements and states they retain ownership unless otherwise stipulated and include notice in service agreements. RA 8293 is the comprehensive IP statute providing the copyright framework, protection duration (life + 50 years), moral rights, and statutory remedies. An architect asserting rights typically relies on both statutes to establish ownership and pursue enforcement.
rationale.takeaway: RA 9266 Section 33 establishes ownership; RA 8293 provides the substantive copyright law framework and enforcement mechanisms.

questions.text: An architectural firm designed a commercial complex and assigned all copyrights to the developer as part of the professional services agreement. Can the architectural firm still enforce copyright against the developer's unauthorized licensing of the design to competitors?

options.text: Yes, because architects always retain moral rights under RA 8293, even after copyright assignment
No, the firm assigned all rights and has no further standing to enforce copyright
Yes, if the unauthorized licensing constitutes a violation of the developer's contractual obligations to the firm
Only if the firm explicitly reserved enforcement rights in the copyright assignment agreement

rationale.b: Ignores the doctrine of inalienable moral rights; the architect retains moral rights even after copyright assignment.
rationale.c: Confuses copyright enforcement with contract breach; after assignment, the developer controls economic copyright, though the architect retains moral rights.
rationale.d: Incorrectly suggests moral rights depend on written reservation; moral rights are inalienable by law regardless of agreement terms.
rationale.correct: Under RA 8293, moral rights (attribution and integrity) are inalienable and cannot be assigned or waived, even when the architect transfers economic copyright rights. The architect retains the right to claim authorship and object to distortions. However, the right to enforce economic copyright (reproduction, distribution) passes to the assignee. The firm cannot sue for infringement based on economic rights, but may assert retained moral rights.
rationale.takeaway: Moral rights (attribution and integrity) are inalienable and remain with the architect even after assigning economic copyright.
